opus-5.5.text:
I think the starting point for me is noticing that science isn't really something that only happens in laboratories. Everyone does it, all the time. A child dropping a spoon off a high chair over and over again is running an experiment. When your car makes a strange noise and you start wondering, is it the brakes, is it the tires, and you try braking gently to see if the sound changes, that's hypothesis testing. We're constantly building little models of the world, making predictions, noticing when those predictions fail, and then intervening to figure out what's actually going on.

What strikes me is how different that is from the way most AI systems learn today. The dominant paradigm is essentially passive. You collect an enormous dataset, you fit a model to it, and the model absorbs whatever statistical regularities are there. That's been remarkably successful, but it's a bit like trying to learn physics purely by reading other people's lab notebooks without ever touching the equipment yourself. You can get very far, but there are certain things that are really hard to learn that way, particularly causal structure. Observational data alone often can't distinguish between "A causes B" and "something else causes both A and B." Intervention is how you break that symmetry.

So the principles I'd like to see shape AI are roughly these. First, the system should be building explicit models of the world, models that have some causal structure, that it can query and reason with, rather than just compressing correlations. Second, it should be active. It should choose what data to gather, design experiments, ask "what would be the most informative thing for me to do right now given what I'm uncertain about?" Third, it should represent its uncertainty honestly. A good everyday scientist knows what they don't know, and that uncertainty is precisely what drives curiosity and exploration. And fourth, it should be able to revise its theories, sometimes radically, when evidence demands it, not just nudge parameters, but actually say "my whole framing of this was wrong, let me try a different structure."

There's a lot of interesting work in probabilistic programming that I think is relevant here, because it gives you a language for expressing rich, structured models of the world and then doing inference over them. You can write a program that says "here's how I think this system works," and then condition on observations and ask what's likely. Combine that with the ability to choose interventions, and you start to get something that looks like an automated scientist in miniature.

And I don't think this is just about building systems that do formal science, although that's an exciting application. It's about general intelligence. The reason humans are so adaptable, why we can walk into a completely unfamiliar situation and figure it out reasonably quickly, is that we have this scientific machinery running all the time. We don't need millions of examples. We form a hypothesis, we poke at the world, and we learn. If we want AI systems that are robust, that generalize to genuinely new situations, that are sample efficient, I think they need to learn the way everyday scientists learn.

r001.rationale: The response recommends explicit causal models and heuristics for active learning, but does not identify humans selecting inductive biases as an input or describe hard-coded knowledge representations.

r002.rationale: It says science is not confined to laboratories and that everyone practices it, then describes everyday hypothesis testing as the scientific machinery that also supports formal science.

r003.rationale: It contrasts active learning with passive training on large datasets and mentions unfamiliar situations, but does not specifically advocate replacing imitation learning to teach interaction with unfamiliar devices or interfaces.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when I say everyday science, I don't mean the institution of science, the labs and the peer review and all of that. I mean the thing that a two-year-old does when they drop a spoon off the high chair for the fiftieth time. They're running an experiment. They have some rough model of how the world works, they're surprised by something, they poke at it, they update. And crucially, they're not just passively absorbing data. They're choosing what to look at, choosing what to intervene on, and building explanations that are structured, causal, compositional.

That's the part I'd really like to see shape how AI systems learn. Right now the dominant paradigm is: take an enormous pile of observational data, fit a very flexible function to it, and hope the regularities you pick up generalize. And that's worked astonishingly well, I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But it's a very different epistemic stance from a scientist, or a child. A scientist doesn't just want to predict the next token of the world. They want a model that explains why things happen, that they can intervene on, that they can transfer to situations that look nothing like the training distribution on the surface but share the same underlying causal structure.

So concretely, a few things I care about. One is that the system should have explicit hypotheses, things that can be true or false, rather than just a big implicit density estimate. Two, the system should be in control of its own data collection to some degree, it should be asking what experiment would most reduce my uncertainty, rather than being fed a fixed dataset. And three, the representations should be compositional and programmatic, because that's what gives you the kind of extrapolation science is good at. If I understand gravity and I understand friction, I can reason about a situation involving both that I've never seen.

That's a lot of why I've spent so much time on probabilistic programming and program synthesis. Programs are a really natural substrate for hypotheses. You can write down a causal model, run it forward, condition on evidence, and ask counterfactuals, and it's all the same object. And at Basis, the organizing idea is essentially that: build systems that reason the way a good scientist reasons, with structured models, with uncertainty, with the ability to design interventions, rather than systems that merely pattern-match on what's already been observed.

I'd also say there's a humility piece in it. Everyday science is comfortable saying I don't know yet, and here's what I'd need to find out. Most of our current systems are not good at that. They're very confident interpolators. I'd like the next generation to be curious rather than confident.

r001.rationale: The response advocates explicit hypotheses, causal models, and programmatic representations, but does not identify human selection of inductive biases or hard-coded knowledge representations and heuristics.

r002.rationale: It presents a child's everyday experiments and a scientist's inquiry as sharing principles such as forming models, responding to surprise, and choosing experiments to update understanding.

r003.rationale: It contrasts observational-data pattern fitting with scientific learning, but does not discuss imitation learning or interactions with unfamiliar devices or interfaces.

astra-6.text:
I’d like AI systems to learn by doing something closer to what we do when we’re trying to understand an unfamiliar situation. We have some idea of how things work, we notice something that doesn’t fit, and we try something to distinguish between possible explanations. That’s a kind of everyday science. It doesn’t require a laboratory; it might just involve figuring out why your bicycle is making a strange noise.

The interesting part is choosing what to do next. If you have two explanations, what observation or intervention would tell them apart? I’d like systems to be able to ask that question, act on it, and revise their understanding when the result surprises them.

And I think that understanding should be something we can examine and challenge. If a system reaches a conclusion, we should be able to ask what assumptions it depends on, what evidence supports it, and what would change its mind. Then learning becomes an ongoing process of constructing and testing explanations, with humans able to participate in that process.

r001.rationale: The response discusses forming and testing explanations, but does not identify human selection of inductive biases or hard-coded knowledge representations and heuristics.

r002.rationale: It describes everyday science, but does not state that everyday and professional scientific inquiry share the same underlying principles.

r003.rationale: It advocates learning through everyday-science-like inquiry, but does not present it as an alternative to large-scale imitation learning for interacting with unfamiliar devices or interfaces.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like AI systems to learn more like we do when we’re trying to figure something out in everyday life. You have some idea of how the world works, you make a prediction, and then you do something that might show you that your idea is wrong. If a light doesn’t turn on, you might change the bulb or check whether something else works in the socket. You’re choosing actions that help distinguish between explanations.

That’s a useful model for learning: build explanations, use them to make predictions, and actively look for evidence that would force you to revise them. The important thing is that the system isn’t just getting better at predicting observations. It’s learning what to investigate next, and how to change its understanding when an experiment doesn’t go as expected.
